newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Tribunal paves way for first mass war crimes trial.
newsitem.headline: Tribunal paves way for first mass war crimes trial.

text.p: A U.N. criminal tribunal gave the go-ahead on Tuesday for its first mass war crimes trial, rejecting a motion from four suspects to be tried separately.
The four, three Moslems and a Croat, are charged with responsibility for war crimes against Serbs at the Celebici camp near Konjic in central Bosnia in 1992.
Two of the Moslems -- deputy camp commander Hazim Delic, 36, and 23-year-old camp guard Esad Landzo -- pleaded not guilty at the U.N. criminal tribunal for former Yugoslavia in June.
Both men were in The Hague court on Tuesday to argue that they should be provisionally released from custody.
The Celebici indictment also names Croat camp commander Zdravko Mucic and Bosnian Moslem military commander Zejnil Delalic.

Delic has denied counts of command responsibility for deaths, tortures and rapes at the camp. He is also accused of taking part in repeated rapes and savage beatings, including one attack when he and Landzo are alleged to have beaten a man with shovels, suffocating him and then burning a cross onto his hand.
Landzo is accused of beating a man while forcing him to do push ups, placing heated metal pincers on the man's tongue and in his ear. He, too, is accused of repeated rapes.
Delic and Landzo were arrested in Sarajevo in April and have been held in tribunal custody in The Hague since June 13.
Mucic was arrested in Austria and pleaded not guilty in The Hague on April 11. Delalic, picked up by German police in March, entered a not guilty plea on May 9.
Delalic had argued that his case would have been prejudiced if evidence against other accused was presented at his trial.
Rejecting the defence move for separate trials, judge Gabrielle Kirk McDonald said: "The interests of justice would clearly be best served by one joint trial."
"Separate trials would...involve much greater delay... considerable repetition of evidence...duplication of testimony and great hardship for already traumatised witnesses."
No date was set for the trial.

The tribunal, the first international body to deal with war crimes since the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials after World War Two, has indicted over 70 Serbs, Croats and Moslems. It holds seven suspects in its Hague cells.
